utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. Mr. Registrar, will you have the accused brought in? (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Registrar, will you have the witness brought in? (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: General, do you hear me? Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Are you ready for us to resume? Have you had a rest?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I'm ready to continue working.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, it's your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Nobilo:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday, at the end of the day's session, we were focusing on document D244, of which you said that it had been written by the commander of the 1st Battalion on the basis of Brigade Commander Cerkez, and the document is D243. Tell me, please, this is a good example of the functioning of the chain of command. Was this customary, or is it a fact that Anto Bertovic was the only educated military officer in the Viteska Brigade, and this was reflected in his adequate military behaviour?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, this order shows the efforts of the commander of the Operative Zone for the chain of command to be fully observed at lower levels, and his persistent efforts to overcome all obstacles on the way to achieving that goal was, obviously, bearing fruit at lower levels already. So the fact that Anto Bertovic, the commander of this battalion, was a trained officer resulted in the order that he received from the brigade being transferred to the subordinates in the battalion as required by military principles and laws of behaviour in the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: May I ask the usher for his assistance?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't recall exactly whether we have authenticated this document. If we haven't, do you recall Cerkez's order and Blaskic's order on the basis of which Cerkez drafted his order? Can you recognise this as implementation of Cerkez's order?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: I remember the order of the commander of the Operative Zone. I personally know the battalion commander Anto Bertovic but, in view of the level of command at which I was engaged and where this order was written, I did not have a chance to see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Could the next document be distributed, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is document D245, D245A for the English translation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We have been talking about the 1st Battalion, the commander of which was Anto Bertovic, the only educated officer in the brigade. Can you cast a glance at this document which was drafted on the same day? As far as you recollect, is this the composition of the 1st Battalion of the Viteska Brigade on the 14th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes. That is the composition of the battalion of which the mentioned officer was the commander, but I should like to comment on a matter that we were focusing on yesterday. You see, in the heading, we see the brigade, but you can also see that the same structure remained, according to the villages: The 1st Company, Nadioci, 20 men; Santici, 12 men; Dubravica, 19; Poculica, 13. What does this mean? It means that you have a company which, if it was a proper military unit, it should have 1st Platoon, 2nd Platoon, 3rd Platoon, but here the units are called after the villages, Nadioci, Santici, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. So these are names of villages in Vitez municipality?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes. You can see what I said yesterday, that our goal was to have a parity structure, that is, to have the proper structure of a brigade. In spite of those efforts, the same problems remained, and that is that the army was organised on the basis of the territorial principle: One village, one unit. As far as I know, at that time, the situation was rather like this also in the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As for the strength, we see that every company should number 92 men, but if we add up these figures, you will agree with me that that envisaged strength was not achieved.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: As far as the numerical strength of the brigades we mentioned yesterday are concerned, I said that in the command we tried to standardise the brigade and to define its permanent size. However, in view of a shortage of military conscripts, we never managed to achieve more than 60 per cent of the envisaged strength of the number established for the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In connection with this, we will distribute a document to see how a brigade was manned.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D246, D246A for the English version.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, we have here the Frankopan Brigade, Guca Gora, Travnik. The date is the 17th of May, 1993. Could you comment, what does this column "envisaged strength" and "actual strength" imply? If you could also comment on the points like the Anti-Armour Battalion, the Artillery Rocket Battalion, where the differences were particularly considerable between the envisaged strength and the actual strength?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: It is visible from this report what the defined structure of the brigade was that we had envisaged at the level of the command of the Operative Zone. That is, that every brigade should number 2.841 men. However, in the far right column where we have the expression "actual strength," we see how the manning actually was. We have the figure for the command, 28, command house, 33, et cetera. When we're talking about the Artillery Rocket Battalion, we manned it with as many men as we had, because it was not rational to have soldiers to man a certain artillery piece if that piece was lacking. In terms of the need to engage the infantry, it was important to have as many men as possible to defend the lines against the Serbs. It is also important to underline the date of this report, and that is the 17th of May, 1993, when, because of the developments in our area, we fully mobilised all available personnel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I should like to draw your attention to point 4. It says, "Communications Company." What was that company doing? What was its task?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: The Communications Company in this brigade had the task of organising communications for the needs of the brigade commander, to organise communications between battalion commanders and the brigade commander using the devices they had at their disposal. I know, in this particular case, in the case of this brigade, because in the course of my regular duties, I occasionally visited this brigade, and I know that they had about 10 telephones and a certain quantity of wire for wire connections. As far as I know, they had one or two automatic telephones and, perhaps, one telefax. In the case of this communications company, they had no other devices. Let me repeat: The Communications Company's duty was to organise communications within the brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it because of the lack of resources that, instead of having 112 men in this company, which should have organised communications upwards and down the command chains, there were only 19. Is that the explanation?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes. That is certainly one of the key reasons, but also in defining the number of men, according to establishment, it is obvious how much importance is attached to communications for the functioning and for implementing commands, and that one of the reasons for planning so many men in this company is this. But the reason why there were only so few, let me repeat, was the shortage of equipment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you confirm the contents of this document and the stamp?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: I can confirm this document, because it was drafted at the request of the commander of the Operative Zone, and it reached the Operative Zone command. On behalf of the commander, it was signed, Brigade Commander Ilija Nakic by Franjo Lujanovic, his assistant for personnel and legal affairs, whom I know personally, and I also know his signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Next document, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D247, and D247A for the English version.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, I will read only two or three lines from this document, which I consider to be important. It was drafted in the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia on the 26th of March, 1993. It is signed by Tihomir Blaskic, and the heading says: "Clarification on Persons Authorised to Appoint and Dismiss Officers and Non-Commissioned Officers." Under point 1, it says: "1) The President of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna is in charge of appointing and dismissing brigade commanders and other high ranking officers. 2) The head of the defence office and the commanders authorised by him appoint and dismiss other officers, that is, persons who have been proposed for these officer posts. 3) The brigade commander may appoint and dismiss the commanders of platoons, squads, and other non-commissioned officers and military staff." Tell me first whether you recognise this document and Blaskic's signature and the stamp of the Operative Zone?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: I am familiar with this document, and it is, indeed, signed by General Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the stamp?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: The stamp is of the command of the Operative Zone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me the circumstances under which this document was written and what was its aim when it was sent to units?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: The document was drafted in the process of transformation of the organisation of units and commands. That was the period when we were setting up brigades, and it came into being in response to questions by our subordinates as to the way to behave administratively regarding proposals for the appointment of commanders in their units. So this is just a part of standard communication when the superior explains certain procedures to his subordinates.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is an instruction, and it is referring to legal regulations in force in Herceg-Bosna at the time. But tell us, did this actually happen in practice or was this the legal framework that efforts were being made to implement?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: I said this is an explanation of administrative procedures as to how proposals should be submitted. Yesterday, when we were talking about actual decision making and appointment of commanders, we said who did it, which means you could make a proposal for the appointment of a brigade commander or the commander of a lower unit if it was approved by the municipal authorities, if we were talking about the municipal level, or a lower level, that would mean the political representatives in the villages. So I'm underlining, this is an explanation of the administrative procedure in implementing legal regulations cited here in the preamble. But what happened in practice, I explained yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can we go on to the next document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Do we have French translations of these documents or will we have them at some point in time?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. The next document has been translated into French, and we have asked the translation section to translate all these documents into both English and French, but there was, indeed, a large number of those documents, and they have been working very hard, and I think they are still working on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you, Mr. Nobilo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Excuse me. Brigadier Marin, you are saying that this document wasn't, in fact, implemented, that this is a theoretical document?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Mr. President and Your Honours, this document that we are referring to now is a clarification to persons of authority, that is, commanders, as to how they should deal with proposals, to whom they should submit proposals for appointments of commanders from the platoon level onwards. So this is an explanation as to how they should work, but we have said how things were in practice. If you wish, I can explain this with an example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: By way of an example, if you wanted to appoint a brigade commander, before doing anything else, the commander of the Operative Zone had to reach agreement with the municipal authorities and to come to an agreement as to the name of the person who would be proposed. When such agreement was reached, information about that commander would be submitted through the brigade commander to the commander of the Operative Zone and further on to the highest level, the president of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. After which, when all these steps were taken, a document would be drafted on the appointment of this commander. Throughout this chain, a key role was played by the political authorities in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So this is not stated at all in these documents. The practice went contrary to the orders, contrary to the administrative documents; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And it was implemented only to appoint or to exclude or dismiss commanders, to put an end to their office. So the authorisation of political authorities at the municipal level was required for that too?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: The definition of standard procedures for the appointment of commanders was the result, or rather, an attempt to build up an organisation on sound foundations under those very difficult conditions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: My question was, how did you dismiss a commander? Was the permission of the municipal authorities required for this too, or could the commander in chief do so directly?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: The approval was required of the municipal authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have the new documents been distributed, please, and what are the numbers, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The next number is D248, 248A for the French translation, and 248B for the English translation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, first, could we have you identify this table? You gave this to me, right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What does it represent and where was it taken from?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: This table is a structure --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Brigadier, is there an English translation of this, counsel? I didn't get one, if I could have one, please. Excuse me. There is none on this sheet here. I apologise, there is one, it's in the same type. I apologise, Mr. President, counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me, please continue now, Mr. Nobilo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, could you tell us, you have given me this document, this table, where were these tables taken from and what do they represent?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: These tables were taken from the manual of NATO and they refer to the structures of command of the corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, you're an officer of the federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina army and now you have are in the process of introducing the NATO standards in the army of federation?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In that connection, you have some translations of certain manuals?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that's exactly where these tables come from. Before we go on, could you clarify for us, what does the first document represent, the first table?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: The first table shows the structure of the command structure of the corps, district.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is district the same as what Operative Zone was in 1993? Are the Operative Zone, the district and corps one and the same thing?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes. I wanted to present this table to the Trial Chamber in order to show what the standards are for the structure of a military district in the NATO organisation with the entire command structure. Also, I would like to compare this table with what the Central Bosnia Operative Zone command had in 1993 and in 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, according to NATO standards, how many officers did Tihomir Blaskic need to have in order to carry out his duties?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: If you look at the first row, first column, and you see the number of officers, he was supposed to have 97 active officers. That is, a total of 151.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The name of this table is "The Table Review of Executives According to the Organisational Units." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Within that table we have a category of officers, non-commissioned officers and soldiers?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then civilians who are employed by the military. Can you tell me how many officers did an Operative Zone need to have, that is according to the NATO standards?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: You can see from this table that the Operative Zone command, according to the NATO standards was supposed to have 151 officers or 235 active duty personnel in total.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I see that two tables are bearing the same title here. We have two tables and in order to facilitate their identification, the first table corresponds to the English translation and it's placed on top. So this is the larger table. The second table is a smaller table, so that can be an orientation for you. One refers to the command of the district and the other one refers to the battalion. Now we are focusing on the table that talks about the district command. So, Brigadier, the district command or the Operative Zone command is supposed to have 151 officers?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many non-commissioned officers?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Seventy-three.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many soldiers?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Two.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many civilian officials?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Twelve.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In total what should be the total personnel according to the NATO standards in an Operative Zone command?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Taken all together, officers, non-commissioned officers of soldiers and civilians, 235.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to remind us, how many persons were in the Operative Zone command?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: As I stated yesterday, I said that we had about 25 persons employed because in those days we did not have ranks. We did not have non-commissioned officers in the HVO structures in those days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said that there were only three persons who had proper military training?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when Omer Bozic was transferred to Kiseljak to the Ban Josip Jelalic brigade, how many of you had left in April?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Colonel Blaskic remained and Ivica Zeko; in other words, two officers remained there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In other words, can we conclude that the number, regardless of the training, but on the basis of what you actually had there, a number of personnel in your command was only 10 per cent of what the NATO standards foresees?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: From everything that we looked at, it is very clear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, let's move on to the next table which shows a motorised Brigade, organisational table.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, maybe just to speed up matters a bit, I think that you're trying now to prove now through your witness, that the military structures were not ones that corresponded to NATO standards or the UN standards. So maybe if we could speed up a bit, obviously, we'll have the right to re-examination in case the Prosecution will contest these points because now we are getting lost in the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's just look at a number of officers and non-commissioned officers in this table. Do you agree with me that it should be 32 officers and 212 non-commissioned officers?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: That is what it states there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many trained officers did Viteska brigade have?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: In the Viteska brigade, there was only one officer who had military training and he did not have full academy training, he just had higher military school training.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D249, 249A for the English translation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, I am going to read several excerpts from this document now. This is the document D249. The title is "The HOS, HSP" and it is sent to the HOS war staff command in Zagreb. It was drafted in Vitez dated July 1992 and the title of the document in "Activity Report." And then we have, 1) the following are under Central Bosnia command: Jajce, Travnik, Novi Travnik, Vitez, Busovaca, part of the Zenica municipality; Cajdras, Fojnica, Kresevo, Kiseljak. That is the Vrbas/Lasva region. In Item 3, the training camp in Vitez has been in existence for four months now, 500 troops have been trained there, and the last item here is Item 5, where it states; we have never -- and never is underlined -- under the command of the TO, the HVO that is, we are the army of the Croatian people and as members of the HOS, we're prepared to lay down our lives for them. Then it is signed, commander of the HOS war staff for Central Bosnia, Major Darko Kraljevic. Can you tell us what this document represents? Are you familiar with the facts that are stated in this document?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, this document is a report of the commander of the HOS units, which in this period, and you see the date there, were operating outside of the HVO organisation -- and later on we will see exactly the timing of that -- were placed under the command of the HVO. I believe that what was stated in Item 3 is incorrect and I think that they are a product of a certain inclination of the lower ranking officers to overblow their contribution. We can also see that this combat formation or unit in reality existed in all these municipalities that are listed here and had its own organisation. You can also see what types of activities this unit was engaged in during the period referred to in this report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So at least in July, as late as July 1992, there were certain Croatian forces which were not within the organisation of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes, and you can see that from this report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, let me take you to a new area now. You talked about the organisation of Brigades. However, in the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, were there also units, organisations, which were outside of the organisation of brigades in the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia? And, if you know, which they were and can you tell us what they are?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Apart from the brigades which have been mentioned, apart from the brigades which have been mentioned, those units which were outside of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone command, there was the PPN unit, Vitezovi, that is special purpose unit, because that was their name. Then there was the military police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, so there was the military police and the special purpose unit called Vitezovi. They both operated within the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, but outside of Operative Zone command organisation?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we move on to the Vitezovi special purpose unit and its structure and organisation, I would like to show you a document which is a report that it sent to its superior command.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document is marked D250, D250A for the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I would like to repeat once again that the documents that are on the ELMO should be available for the public gallery to see. I have asked for it several times. It is not so difficult because even the defence has stated all the documents should be put on the ELMO. Please choose one of the official languages of the Tribunal to do it. Usually it's in English, but we have got public hearings now, so that the public can be able to follow in an appropriate manner this trial. Because the public, otherwise, they know who is speaking, whether Mr. Nobilo or myself. They can show from time to time the speaker, but when we are discussing a particular document, I would like that on the ELMO the cameras show what is on the ELMO and that should be in one of the two official languages of the Tribunal. I would like not to have to repeat it any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I have understood.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is a long report, and I'm only going to read several excerpts which, I believe, are relevant to establish the chain of command or the line of command. Let me read. This is the 18th of February, 1994, to the office of the main headquarters of the HVO of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, to Ms. Mirjana Loncar personally. "Following the order of Colonel Darko Kraljevic, Commander of the PPN Vitezovi, issued on 15 February, 1994, we submit to you this report," and in the first sentence it states: "The unit, PPN Vitezovi or the Special Purpose Unit Vitezovi, was established on 10 September, 1992 pursuant to the decree about the armed forces of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna." The last paragraph on the first page, this is the last paragraph. "Following the order of Brigadier Milivoj Petkovic, Chief of the Main Headquarters of the HVO, issued on 14 October, 1992, the Commander of the Special Purpose Unit Vitezovi, Darko Kraljevic, issued the order 1-073/92 of 15th of October regarding sending 60 soldiers of the special purpose unit to Grude." On the next page, page number 2, in the second paragraph in the Croatian original, it states: "On 24 October, 1992, after the outburst of hostilities between the HVO and the ABiH, Defence Minister Bruno Stojic ordered that the team return to the area of Central Bosnia." On page 3, after "The Year 1993," that is the heading --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I would like to ask the usher, when the counsel announces a version of a page, it is the page that is in the Croatian version and also, very often, in English, so please put the appropriate page on the ELMO. Please stay next to the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So under "The Year 1993" heading, it states: "Following the order of the Chief of the Main Headquarters of the HVO, number 01-66/93, of 15 January, 1993, the Special Purpose Unit Vitezovi was put in a state of mobile readiness of the highest degree." On the next page, this is page 4 of the Croatian document, paragraph 5, it states --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Excuse me. The interpreters are looking for the text.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will repeat the text. It is page 4 of the Croatian original, paragraph 5. "The report number 2-091/93 of 15 March, 1993 was sent to the Head of the Department of Defence, Mr. Bruno Stojic, and to the Chief of the Main Headquarters of the Croatian Army, Brigadier Milivoj Petkovic. It reported about the activities of the Vitezovi Special Purpose Unit during the conflicts in Central Bosnia." On page 6 of the Croatian text ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Nobilo, but when a text is so long, not only the public has to be able to follow, but also the Prosecutors as well. I think that maybe if it's a longer text, it would allow also the usher to put it on the ELMO, and also, the counsel for the Prosecution would also be able to follow it a bit better. Generally, I'm trying to speed up our debate, but when a document is long, we also must be able to have a proper reference. When you say "page 6, paragraph 3 of the Croatian text," could you please find the proper references in English, and I will find it for myself later on. Also, I think the interpreters are thanking me as well, which is perfect.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: That is correct, Mr. President. It is a bit complicated. However, I think we have the exact text which I would like to read. This is paragraph 2, and it starts, "Following the order number," and so on. We have it on the screen, and I believe the interpreters will be able to handle it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: This is what page? Unfortunately, the English version hasn't got any page numbers, but it seems to be page 6 of the English version, starting "Following the order of the commander." Thank you. In that case, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes. If you'll look at the monitor, I know that in the Croatian version, it is page 6, but I see the corresponding page in English. Let me read it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "Following the order number 01-10/78/93 of the Commander of the General Corps, Colonel Tihomir Blaskic," and we don't see the numbers particularly well. "The Vitezovi Special Purpose Unit took over the control and defence of Zabrdze, but not in its entirety, because two-thirds of it were already under the control of the Muslim armed forces." Then on the same page, I'll read the last paragraph. It starts with "Communication." It's the next page of the English translation where it refers to communication, so it is at the very top. It's actually the first full paragraph. "We had practically no communication with our superiors in that period of time. We were forced to handle the paperwork the way we supposed it should be done, as nobody among us had the professional knowledge needed for such work. Each time we called the General Corps and asked for instructions, the answer was short and similar, 'Call Mostar.'" Let me mention again, it is well-known how the communication lines worked back then. Then it is signed by the Deputy Commander of the Special Purpose Unit Vitezovi, Major Dragan Binac. I would like to take you back to the first page of this report. Could you just answer very precisely the questions which I asked of you? Why does the Vitezovi unit send a report about its work for the year '92 and '93 to the main command of the Croatian Defence Council of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna? Will you please tell us what is the main headquarters of the HVO and why is this report addressed to them?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, the main headquarters of the HVO is the highest level of command of the HVO of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the report we are talking about is addressed to the main headquarters and not the Operative Zone, because this unit was not under the direct command of the commander of the Operative Zone, and it was not part of the organisational structure, which included the other units coming under the command of the Operative Zone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then we go on to the next question. Under the title "Report," it says that the Vitezovi unit was formed on 10 September, 1992. Was that the date when the HOS unit, from document 249, joined the HVO or is it something new?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes. That was the time when the HOS units in Bosnia-Herzegovina became part of the organisational structure of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have read out several orders which I consider to be relevant. Let me now just repeat that the HOS received, from the Chief of Staff of the Main Headquarters, Milivoj Petkovic, which is the paragraph at the top of the second page of the English translation, which reads -- my learned friend is marking it -- that an order is received on the 14th of October, 1992 from the Chief of the Main Headquarters, Brigadier Milivoj Petkovic. After that, it is said that on the 24th of October, 1992, they received orders from Defence Minister Bruno Stojic. Then in 1993, on the 15th of January, just under the title "The Year 1993," page 4 of the English translation, on the 15th of January, they are still receiving orders from the chief of the main headquarters of the HVO in Herzegovina. Then a couple of paragraphs further down, on the 15th of March, they receive orders from Milivoj Petkovic and Bruno Stojic or, rather, they are reporting to them about their work, that is, to Milivoj Petkovic and to Bruno Stojic. Page 5 of the English translation, the top of the page that is now on the screen, they are sending a report on the 15th of March, 1993 to the Head of the Department of Defence, Bruno Stojic, and the Chief of the Main Headquarters, Milivoj Petkovic. The first order that they received from Tihomir Blaskic that they mention has the number 01-10/78/93, and as the middle figure indicates the month, it means October, the month of October. On the basis of all that we have read so far and all your knowledge, can you comment on the status of the Special Purpose Unit Vitezovi and what came under its command?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: The PPN Vitezovi Special Purpose Unit, as I have said, was outside the organisational structure of the command of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone. It was under the direct command of the Ministry of Defence of Herceg-Bosna, but it was placed under the operative command of the commander of the Operative Zone. Such a situation, in terms of command, further complicated or made difficult control over those forces, and it also made difficult their assignment to combat duty. The order made by the commander of the Operative Zone in 1993 was issued at a time when we were totally surrounded, and one might say we had no communications or, rather, no quality communications with the main headquarters, and because of the possibility given to use those forces operatonally, the commander of the Operative Zone did issue a specific combat assignment to the Special Purpose Unit Vitezovi.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, Brigadier, in very simple and clear terms, Colonel Tihomir Blaskic, in military terms, could he directly give orders to the Vitezovi? Would they obey those orders or was this done in another way?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: The commander of the Operative Zone was not in a position to be able, directly, to give orders or to give assignments to the Vitezovi Special Purpose Unit. But before issuing an order, he first had to contact the commander of the PPN Vitezovi Special Purpose Unit, persuade him that the task he intends to assign to him is indispensable, and only after that was he able to write an order and send it to the mentioned commander. That was the situation in practice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, in formal and legal terms, special purpose units in Herceg-Bosna, including Vitezovi, did they have a special status in relation to brigades, and were they directly linked to the Defence Ministry?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes. They had a special status, and, as far as I'm aware, they also had separate logistics support.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, Brigadier, could Colonel Blaskic, in any way, appoint or dismiss the commander of a special purpose unit?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: No, because all personnel affairs, logistic affairs, came under the terms of reference of the Defence Ministry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell the Court, could Colonel Blaskic and the disciplinary court and the prosecutor's office, could it punish members of the PPN unit?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: No. We did not have the necessary competence for this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you explain the fact that Colonel Blaskic did, as frequently as he could, issue written orders to the Vitezovi, as well as to all other brigades?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: These efforts best reflect the extent to which General Blaskic tried to structure the army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you mean to say that he wouldn't reconcile himself to such a state of affairs or, rather, what was your opinion?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Counsel. The question should be asked as to what was meant, not what Mr. Nobilo wants it to mean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No. I think Mr. Nobilo was just about to put his questions. Mr. Nobilo, please continue. You have a lot of questions about the Vitezovi left?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Just one or two and then we will finish this area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, your expert opinion, in accordance with the principles of command, was this, according to your professional opinion, an error in the organisational structure or was it acceptable?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: In my opinion, this was an error in the organisation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the opinion of Colonel Blaskic at the time?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Colonel Blaskic never reconciled himself with the fact that we had a poor organisation, that the structure was not adequately developed, and he tried everything in his power to improve the organisation and structure and make it more effective. These written orders had a twofold role. One was to have written traces, written documents, to show what measures had been taken. The second was that the people who were in command of those units and those forces should be trained and taught how things should be done. A third point I should like to stress were the efforts that he made to improve the structure and the organisation, because he wanted to make progress. He wanted to create an army that would be ready and capable of defending the defence lines towards the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My last question about Vitezovi: In addition to these legal problems, were there any factual problems due to the fact that the Vitezovi were local men, and who could bring influence to bear on them, in view of this fact that they were locals?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes. This unit consisted of men who did, indeed, make a major contribution on the battlefront from the very first days of combat with units of Republika Srpska. In view of this contribution they made, all these men, and especially their commander, the late Colonel Darko Kraljevic, in the environment in which he lived, enjoyed respect from the inhabitants and the politicians. He was revered. Such a situation, additionally, made difficult the implementation of the commands because the situation made it possible for members of this unit to have greater leeway in their behaviour. Another point I wish to make is the fact that they were directly responsible to the Defence Ministry. Us being physically separated from the Defence Ministry also made it impossible for us to fully control the situation in that unit and the implementation of its tasks. This is something that both the members and the commanders used very skilfully in the following way: If the commander, Colonel Blaskic, gave an assignment to that unit and, in their view, this didn't really suit them, then they would simply say, "We have to contact Mostar," and then they would find all kinds of excuses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, I think we've explained sufficiently the position of that unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: It is also time to break, in view of our interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. We are going to have a 15-minute break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, let the accused be brought in. Mr. Nobilo, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, we will stay slightly more on the document D250. There are just a few words I would like to say about this. This document has been addressed to the Defence office and on the last page it is written to whom this has been sent to, to the addressee and to the unit PPN Vitezovi. Did you receive this report in the Operational Zone? I stress this is a report made in 1994.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes, we did receive this report, which can be seen from the receiving stamp on page 1 in the top corner, but we received it on the 25th of February, 1994, although it had been written on the 18th of February, 1992 (sic). I do not know under what circumstances this report had arrived to the command of the Operational Zone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Vitezovi very often send reports to you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: During the whole time of the war it happened very rarely. We could say we hardly received any operational reports or any other reports about the situation in that unit and the activities of that unit and of other features, characteristics for that unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I ask the assistance of the usher now.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document is marked D251.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, before we have a look at this document, perhaps it would be better to centre it on the ELMO first. Yes, thank you. Could you now tell us something about the military police and its status?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Can we put it also on the ELMO so that the public gallery can see it? This is not a very complex document. No, we are going to start only when the public gallery will be able to see it. Now you can proceed, Mr. Nobilo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Chairman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we start analysing this document, you mentioned there were two structures outside of the brigade and outside of the Operational Zone: one was the Vitezovi and the other was the military police. What was the state of the military police in the Operational Zone in central zone?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: The military police, together with the command of the Operational Zone of Central Bosnia was under the operative command of the commander of the Operative Zone. It was not part of the organisational structure of the Operational Zone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell me what it means, "operational commanding"?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Operational commanding in the simplest terms means that a particular unit, a unit with a particular status and that unit is given to you, so you can use it in an operation. The commander can use a particular unit for carrying on particular tasks when it comes to the military police. In this case, the commander of the Operational Zone could order them to carry out operational and military police activities, for example, monitoring.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, apart from this operational use of the military police, was there a direct line of command of the military police towards another body?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: The military police was in its organisational form linked to the Ministry of Defence, and whatever was linked to the military police was done through that line chain of command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who appoints and dismisses commanders in the military police?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: That authority was upon the department of defence of the Ministry of Herceg-Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When it came to disciplinary punishment, was it under the organisation of the Operational Zone of Central Bosnia or did they have their own system of disciplinarian punishment?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Disciplinarian punishment was not in the competence of the Operational Zone, it was dependent on the military police board.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Some purely police activities, for example, investigations about criminal deeds and similar activities, was there a direct chain of command towards the administration of the military police and the defence department?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the military police obliged to inform the commander of the Operational Zone or was it obliged only to make reports to its superiors?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: The military police was not obliged to inform the commander of the Operational Zone, but it had to inform the military police superiors.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All the logistics of the military police, the weapons and the other supplies, could it rely on its own logistics?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes, military police had its own logistics. The military district, that is the Operational Zone, provided it with food and with fuel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, let us now look at this schematic, this is D251. I would also like the cameras to show it to the public gallery. Would you please explain to me, what does this schematic represent? Can you also explain to us what are direct and what are subsidiary lines of commands?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, from this schematic, we can see the complete organisational structure of the HVO, from the defence department --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a moment, Brigadier. Let us first look at line 2. We have a title, the "Croatian Defence Council." And then the 5th line there, did it really mean that those were like ministries in the Government of Herceg-Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was under the defence department under the Ministry of Defence of the Government of Herceg-Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: We can see from this schematic that under the Ministry of Defence, there was the command of the military police, the main headquarters of the HVO and the security department.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the main headquarters of the HVO, what was directly under it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Directly under the main headquarters of the HVO were the Operational Zones. That is the commands of the military districts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And directly under the third Operational Zone, this was the Operational Zone of Central Bosnia, which is the issue in this case, which units were under it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: We can see from the schematic that these were the brigades, Vitez, Kafron Vitez (phoen), Banja Letic (phoen) from Kiseljak --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the others were mentioned yesterday?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes, the ones we answered yesterday and also some additional units like us, the air defence one and the artillery and rocket division.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. If we analyse now units which were in Central Bosnia, do you agree with me when I say that these were all units that are here in the same row here on this schematic as the markings for the third zone, the Operational Zone of Central Bosnia? I'm sorry, not all the units, but the units Vitezovi. I am going to correct myself and rephrase the question. Could you explain on the schematic, the status of the unit Vitezovi?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: The status of this unit, Vitezovi, we can see from the schematic, we've got a line here, a full line, which represents direct subordination and we can see from here that that unit was under the Ministry of Defence. And there is a cut line, interrupted line, represents operational subordination, which depended on the command of the Operational Zone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We can see this twofold commanding structure here. Let us now look at the Operational Zone of Central Bosnia. We've got here the 4th battalion of the military police, can you explain to us these two lines of command?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: The vertical chain of command here, it was the administration and the command of the military police that was in control and the operational use was something that was the possibility of the commander of the Operational Zone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We can see that here. It is a dotted line that represented. Now, my colleague will mark in pink this vertical chain of command regarding the 4th battalion of the military police. There was another service, not a unit, but a service called SIS, that they also have these two chains of command, a direct one and a subsidiary one?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes, we can see it from the schematic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My learned colleague is now going to draw in blue that particular service and that particular chain of command. Does this schematic faithfully represent what you have just told us now concerning these two chains of command?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes, I can stress it and I can say that this was, to my mind, an error in the structure, organisational structure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, we've talked about the organisation of Brigades. You said that the organisational forms were very often changed. Tell us, once the brigades were founded to replace the municipal staffs and so on, did all these negative impacts, consequences happen after that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: No, we still had those key problems. Those were the local influences on the commanders. We still had elements of voluntariness because we had no instruments by which we could oblige a particular mission to be carried out. Also, the units still remained organised on a village system, which we could see from one of the tables, which we saw today where villages were lifted. So these crucial, essential problems still remained. By trying to find new structural forms of organisation, the commander of the Operational Zone attempted to find the best solutions which would guarantee a proper functioning of the organisation, as should be the case when it comes to commanding and organising.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, you were one of the closest collaborators at the time of Colonel Blaskic, what did he spend most of his working day on in 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: It is correct that I was one of the closest collaborators of General Blaskic. Such was my duty. But 90 per cent of his working day, of the working day of General Blaskic, he used to organise the military structured organisation, which would efficiently defend the front-line with Republic of Srpska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Apart from the efficiency that could be the result of a better organisational structure, why did General Blaskic insist so much on the organisational structure? Were this any other reasons for it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: It is logical that if you have a good structure and organisation, there would be less breaches of discipline and everything will be done more efficiently and in a better way. Apart from the purely military task, all these other things are also very important and General Blaskic had that in mind and took steps in order to limit them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, you're an officer of the army of the federation, it is well known that for a number of years MPRI, a professional military company, together with the help of the United States is trying to form a better situation in the Croatian and Muslim forces in the federation. When they arrived in 1996, and when they made a case study of the situation in the HVO, what were the suggestions and what did they find?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: 1995 was the year when we made in the HVO a number of steps forward as compared to 1992. It is known to me because I have participated in the meetings with MPRI when they presented some key problems which still existed in the HVO in 1995. We have probably improved somewhat on those problems in 1996. The problems were the following: A bad functioning of the system of command; no good facilities in terms of lodgings for the military and the problems of financing of the army. These were the three facts that were found by MPRI company when they made a study of the organisation of that army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that in 1995 MPRI, so two to three years after this event, said that the HVO did not have a proper system of commanding. What did that organisation think how -- much time will it need for the army of the federation, after which HVO is a part to build an army on the status of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: What is MPRI?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Brigadier Slatko Marin will probably be able to explain that much better than I can because I know only a few things about the organisation.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, MPRI is an international organisation that is part of the Government of United States of America and its task is to form and organise the army of the federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. In that organisation works retired officers of the United States of America, which had received the task I was just speaking of, our government has accepted that form of cooperation and we now cooperate very intensely on the build-up of the army of the federation together with that organisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the conclusions that were made by this organisation, the three facts that were found.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, could you please tell the Court once again what were the three main problems in the HVO found by this American organisation in 1995?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, the company I was speaking of found the following: The HVO has got problems because it has not have a proper system of control and command. Number two, non-existence of facilities in terms of lodging for a professional army. That means that we have no barracks. Number three, financial problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, that was in 1995. Until what year does this programme of training of the army of the federation last in order for them to be able to fulfil the requirements of modern military standards?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: According to what I mentioned, it will be necessary up until 2003 to work very intensely so that the army of the federation could function on the basis of well-known military standards according to which function all European armies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So ten years after the event we're speaking of?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes, more or less so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, could you please tell the Court, during the war between Croats and Muslims in Central Bosnia, before the war and during that war, what frontlines towards the Serbs were held by the HVO? Could you please go to the map and explain which defence lines were held?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: We have to change the slide and the following slide will show the situation as it was then in the field.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please explain the symbols? Can you tell us where the Serb lines were and where the Croatian lines were?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Just a few items of information about this map. This map is on the scale 1:100.000. What does it mean that 1 centimetre on this map represents 1 kilometre in nature. I am saying this so that you can have the best possible representation of the situation on the ground. What you can see here is that in red are the positions of the army of Republic of Srpska. In green we see the deployment of the units of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, also the position of the BH army towards the Serbs. In blue we can see the defence lines held by the HVO, and hereby I stress since the beginning of 1992, even more precisely, since March 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, there where you have a red line, which means a line of the army of Republic of Srpska and a blue line next to it is not straight next to it, can we say that this line is held by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me, we should show the map for the public gallery.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, now the public gallery can also see the map. So blue lines, the HVO; the red lines the Serbs and the green lines represent the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Please go on, Brigadier.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: I will try the explain and clarify the positions of the HVO as towards army of Republic of Srpska. In Central Bosnia, municipalities of Travnik, Novi Travnik, Bugojno, Tomislavgrad and Ilano (phoen). From Livno, that means practically from the Croatian border, following this blue line through Bugojno, up until just before the village of Prusac, all this line was held by the HVO units. The green line on the Municipality of Bugojno, part of it, were held by the units of the BH army. Furthermore, the line that goes in front of the Municipality of Novi Travnik and up until the point I am showing now to the village of Busta (phoen). Busta was also held by the HVO. Then from Busta to Turbe, that was held by the army of BH army. Then from Turbe up to Vlasic, this is the hill feature, Vlasicka Gromila. That was also held by the HVO unit. This is part of the battle front that was towards the Republic of Srpska. Furthermore, this blue line going just to Zepce, it is also where we held the defence lines towards Republic of Srpska Zepce. I apologise, there is something that I omitted here from Vlasicka Gromila and to Zenica we can see in green lines that those defence lines were held by the units of the BH army. Something else which we cannot see here because this map does not represent it, there also existed another line at Usora towards the frontlines of Republic of Srpska. Now we're going on to the area of Vares. Near the town of Vares we had this line as shown here towards the front-line with Republic of Srpska. Then we go on to Kiseljak and we can see there we also have frontlines with Republic of Srpska army. It is true that all the defence lines of the HVO are not shown here. For example, in eastern Herzegovina. It would have been technically impossible to represent it on a map of this scale and to my mind, it would be important, in this particular case, to show this particular section of the map with the Operational Zone of Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Both armies, Croat and the Muslim army had frontlines with the army of the Republic of Srpska, could you now draw a conclusion from the characteristics of the deployment of the BH army which at least, so it seems to me, held defence lines and is more deployed in depth of the territory of Central Bosnia. Can you explain to us this deployment?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: The focus of the HVO, the way the work was organised starting in 1992 was to deploy towards the troops of the Republic of Srpska army, and everything was geared towards that end. From this map you can see and this is indeed how things were, the available forces which held the positions on the front-line. You can see from here that it was a small line of defence and it does not correspond to the actual forces which were deployed in the Central Bosnia area. Now, let me give you an example, like Novi Travnik, you see the line. So for this entire municipality, you see this is the area because we did say before that the army was organised on the territorial principles. So in this area, we don't have any BH army forces. However, the BH army did have a presence in the Novi Travnik area, but not on the front-line. They were deployed in the depth of the territory which is where they were organised and which was where they were structured, and they would just deploy within the area. In this way, the army would in that way gain more and more control over the area behind the frontlines towards the Serbian army. That would be behind the HVO backs, the HVO which held those defence lines against the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the conflict between the Muslims and the Croats from April 1993 until February 1994, that is, the Washington Agreement, did the HVO, at any given time, voluntarily abandon the frontlines towards the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: The defence lines, which were assumed in 1992, after we had stopped the Chetnik -- I'm sorry, the Bosnian Serb army troops was kept until June of 1993, that is, until the time when the BH army units attacked members of the HVO units which were holding the positions towards the troops of the army of Republika Srpska. So at that time, in June of 1993, the HVO withdrew from the positions in the area of Travnik and Novi Travnik, because this area was now placed under the control of the BH army, and the HVO was pushed back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, Brigadier, I'm going to take you to a new area which, I believe, is crucial to these proceedings, and I believe that your expertise will be significant for this Trial Chamber when they evaluate the evidence. I want to ask you some things about the organisation of command. First of all, what are the basic characteristics which guide the control and command in any structured and organised army?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: The main function, that is, in order for a system of command control to be operational are as follows: Planning, organisation, command, coordination, supervision, and control. Those are the basic functions which any command and control system must have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Let's go to the control now, and let's try to see what the situation was in Central Bosnia Operative Zone. First we have planning or forecasting. What does that mean? Can you just clarify this for the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Planning, as one of the basic characteristics of command and control, is activity of the commanding officer and the command whereby he has to or they have to forecast, they have to prognosticate, and then act on that. That is at the level -- this planning was not implemented formally, either at our command or the subordinate levels. As I mentioned, this was due to the lack of trained personnel who would be able to do this forecasting in a way that a trained officer may be able to do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Second, the organisation of work of the command and units, what can you say about that, briefly?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Any commander, when he lays down the basic organisational work, first of all, he's going to plan, and once you have completed your planning, once you have made your estimates and you have -- you are now ready to proceed to establish a particular organisation to accomplish this task. I have already testified to how much organising work we have done through this period, for our main objective, which was the defence against the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, do you think that during the war you were not successful in building the organisation, the military organisation, which would effectively accomplish the tasks set out by your commander?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes. That is correct. We did not build up the organisation which would carry out all the tasks that were before us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Next, I want to take you to the command. What are the forms of command?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: When you have reached a decision, when you have planned, when you have built an organisation, then you proceed to the commanding itself. We see that the command in the Operative Zone was carried out through written orders and many, many times, a commander of the Operative Zone insisted orally, verbally, so he was given oral orders to his subordinates in order to carry out certain tasks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your judgement, orders which were written by Mr. Blaskic and his associates, were they of better standard than the other orders which were issued by others?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes. That is correct. They were clear. They were unequivocal. It was clear who was supposed to carry out what task, how they were going to do it. However, the conditions in which these orders were written were such as we have explained earlier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is the supervision or monitoring of the implementation of these orders, can you explain to the Tribunal what was the significance of the monitoring and supervision?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: If you had set up an organisation, you had issued commands and orders, the next part of the activity is to ensure that everything was carried out. So you needed to monitor and supervise, and these are key factors in the command organisation. If you are not able to have your orders carried out, the extent to which these orders are carried out, if the quality of the job, if you are not able to supervise, if you are not able to monitor that, if you are not able to control that, then it was all in vain. If you are not able, by supervising, to arrive at additional steps and measures that need to be taken, your task would not have been accomplished. So control and supervision is very important.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you, what were the specific problems which were cropping up in the Operative Zone, especially in the enclaves which were physically separated from the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: The key problem in the area which was the responsibility of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, the command problem was that precisely because of the physical separation, we were not able to go into the area and verify and control directly how things were implemented there. It was only directly through reports and through other communications that we were able to do so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you maintain control through irregular reports, how is that reflected and how do you get a real picture of what is going on on the ground?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: If you are not able to directly verify on the ground how certain orders were carried out, and if such information comes to you through written orders, through these reports, you will never be able to find out fully how certain orders were carried out and what is the actual situation at a particular line of defence. Because a local commander will write from his own vantage point, and it is clear that it would be very positive, because he knows that you cannot actually control him, because physically, you cannot go there and do the verifying process yourself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the role of coordination?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Coordination is another important factor, because all the operations take place in an area where you have civilian authorities, you have religious authorities. There is a lot of organisation, a lot of coordination that needs to be done with respect to other institutions which are around you and with whom you have contacts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me specifically what needs to be done to make certain orders carried out efficiently?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: In order to fully understand the process of command and control, all these functions, which I have here mentioned, need to be carried out cumulatively. In other words, all of them have to be fully carried out, and that is prerequisite for full control of a commander over the situation. If any one of these factors is missing, then the whole system has been interrupted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, what are the principles of command that any commander needs to know when carrying out his duties?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: The principles of command are also extremely important, and let me try and numerate them for you. It is the unity of command, subordination, the principle of single command confidentiality, and operational factors.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were all these principles which are supposed to be implemented in every military organisation also implemented in the Central Bosnia Operative Zone?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me, what would happen if the chain of command of the Operative Zone in an enclave was broken, let's say in Zepce or else where? What would happen then?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: In principle, one of the principles is the continuation, the continuity of command and control. In the military structure of units, a unit must never be left without a commander. If the communication is lost, the next superior commander takes over responsibility for the maintaining of the line of defence for carrying out all the tasks in the zone of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also said confidentiality. What was the confidentiality or secrecy about the command of the Operative Zone regarding any enclaves which were physically separated from the Operative Zone command? I mean communications lines. Did you have means which would guarantee this confidentiality?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: No. We did not have such means, and the level of confidentiality, therefore, was very, very low.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you allow yourself the luxury, for instance, that a commander in Kiseljak would send you the exact deployment of his troops, what would that mean, given the means of communications which you had available?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: That would mean, in practical terms, that he was sending this same information to the enemy. We only had means of communications which were at amateur level. They could be deciphered. If there were any codes, they could be listened to, and no commander could allow himself the luxury to give the information on his forces to the enemy's side. If you will allow me, in such situations, the reports and tasks which we exchanged were, for the most part, general and would not contain specific information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, could you be specific? What would the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, or any other enemy, what would they do if they received this information on the full deployment or complete deployment?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: They would take certain steps, and they would threaten the forces which were on the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, I think that we can go on without being really military strategists. I think that if somebody manages to intercept your communications, I think that it is pretty obvious that it will have negative consequences for the ones whose communication was intercepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I thought it would be useful to just discuss some of the military theory here, but let me move on. I have the next document. Can I have it distributed, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, see, we thought that maybe we could have a 15-minute break at 12.25. I'm now going to tackle a new subject, or maybe it would be a better moment to have a break now?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: In that case, we will have a 15-minute break.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes. This is a good idea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, do you plan to complete your examination-in-chief at 1.30 because we will not be going on after that? We will be resuming work on Monday at two. I was just asking Mr. Nobilo whether he plans to finish today? No, on Monday?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: We don't believe so, Mr. President, because this is an extremely important witness. We have a large number of documents, but we will probably need two more working days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I was just trying to learn what your plans are, so that the Prosecution can organise themselves as well. In that case, we will adjourn at 1.30 sharp and resume on Monday at two. So please continue now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I think we've distributed a new document, a schematic, could I have the number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The new document has been marked D252.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, could you please explain to the Court what this schematic represents?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, this schematic shows the levels of command in the Croatian Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean in the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes, as a part of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you tell the Court, between the commander of the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia, Tihomir Blaskic, and a group of soldiers on the attack, who are deciding whether to throw a grenade into the left-hand house or the house on the right, how many levels of command are there in between?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: The commander of the Operative Zone was at the operative level of command. And the subordinate commanders had the tactical level of command.
