When the commander of the Operative Zone would issue a command in the chain of command, for that order to reach a group of soldiers or a particular soldier it had to pass through the following levels of command: the brigade commander, then the battalion commander, the platoon commander, the squad commander and finally the group commander. Then that leader of the group would issue the order to a group or an individual.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Between the commander of the Operative Zone and the Brigade commander, we also have commanders of operative groups that you would form occasionally, what did they represent? How is an operative group organised? Who is its commander and the command of that group as a whole?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: With the establishment of operative groups, their establishment reflected the need for more effective control and command of units and defence. They were formed under conditions when the army of Republic of Srpska was exerting strong pressure on the defence lines and it was then that we undertook to form these operative groups as I described yesterday. When we are talking about our operative groups, in our case, an operative group in the HVO, it didn't have a separate command, though, according to the rules in a well-organised army, it should have. However, in our case, the commander of the operative group was taken over by the command of the strongest Brigade in that area. So that in Kiseljak we had the commander of the Banja Luka Brigade, who was also commander of the operative group. The activities within that operative group are under the commander of the command of that operative group. The same applied to other operative groups.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, in the army, is it possible and is it customary for the commander of an Operative Zone to give a command to the smallest unit? To a squad? Or did that order have to go through various levels of subordinate commanders?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: If any such act were to be undertaken, that would be undermining the whole system of subordination. I do not know of a case of a commander from such a high level, especially in a structured army, to give a command the squad commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean, will you explain to the Court, when a commander of an operative zone issues an order then all of these levels must issue a new order on the basis of this original order; is that so?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you tell the Court, the reports coming from the ground, the assault group says we threw a hand grenade into a house on the left because they shot at us and not at the house on the right because they didn't shoot at us, how does the report reach the commander of the Operative Zone?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: The report has to go up the chain of command the other way around then. The squad will support the commander of the platoon, the platoon commander, the company commander, the company commander, the battalion commander, the battalion commander, the operative group commander and the operative group commander, the commander of the operative zone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happens if anyone in that chain of command fails to execute his duties or does so inadequately?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: In the case of reporting, the report will be incomplete, poor in quality and it will not provide sufficient information to the commander of the Operative Zone as to the situation on site, where the battle is being waged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, an order coming from the level of the Operative Zone, what happens with it? Or maybe it would be a better idea for me to read an order and then you can tell me what type of an order it is, from what level it is coming. Central Bosnia command is writing to the brigade commander in Zepce. First of all, the enemy is defined and it says in point 1: After the regrouping of forces and supply of equipment, the enemy will intensify its combat activities with the principle goal of pushing back our forces --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I am wondering, Mr. Nobilo, you're reading a document that was not given to anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: That is correct, Mr. President. I just wanted to read a document which is a typical order issued by the Operative Zone level. Then I wanted the brigadier to tell us whether this was indeed a typical order. The facts are not important, just the type of order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I don't mind, but I wonder if the Prosecution agrees with this procedure? Mr. Kehoe, are you in agreement with this procedure or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I really am not. With all due respect, counsel, it's just as difficult to follow without the actual written document. I am going to ask if you're going to read something that everybody be given a copy so that we can all follow along.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Unfortunately we don't have an English translation. But let me rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Never mind, try and find a way out. You have been speaking alone with so many documents, but that is not exactly in accordance with the procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I have put away the document and we'll try and do without it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Perhaps that would be better, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, tell me from the level of the Operative Zone, what do combat orders look like?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, the commander of an Operative Zone, I said that this was the operative level, and in his orders he issues assignments to his subordinates in which he gives the global assignments by way of example, a unit or an operative group has the task of organising defence along this front-line. So the commander of the Operative Zone will assign the task to organise defence left or right. You have a feature there, another one there. You have to hold the enemy and defend the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he will indicate the limits?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: The borders of the zone of responsibility and a global assignment, defend it or attack it, then the brigade commander will define what the task of the battalion is. Then the battalion commander will determine what the task of the company is and so on. As I said, the commander of the Operative Zone gives the global principle task; whereas the lower level commanders determine the place, the time and the forces or units that have to carry it out. If we've come to the platoon commander, then he will say such and such a feature needs to be captured, or control over it needs to be achieved, or it needs to be protected. In that order, that feature is clearly defined. It is in most cases a hill or a building or a particular point in the relief, which is recognisable in that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Using my example of houses on the left and on the right, who decides at what house a hand grenade will be thrown?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: It is either the leader of the squad or, in most cases, in fact, a small group with three or four soldiers in it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D253, D253A for the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I wanted to ask, in document D252, on the right-hand side of the page, it says, "Amount of destruction in villages." Do you want to talk about that too, because you didn't mention it at all, and it appears in the document, Loncari, and so on. What is that about?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Your Honours, we will be talking about that a little later. When we come to the specific events, we will be coming back to this level of command and carry out a military analysis. We didn't comment on it at this stage, but we will do so later on in our case when the time comes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, please take a look at this document. It is brief, and for the benefit of the public, I would like to read it. It says: "Commander Mijo Bozic from Kiseljak, on the 9th of March, 1993, to the Command of the Operative Zone in Vitez." He is obviously giving an explanation, and he says: "Further to order, strictly confidential number 01-4-36/93 item 1, of 7 April, 1993, and due to the insecurity of the passage to Vitez and the degree of secrecy of that order, we cannot send it to you, even though it stands under number 011-767-1/93." Tell us, how did this reach Vitez, in view of the stamp that we see on the original?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: You mean this explanation?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. The explanation, how did it reach Vitez, and can you explain the stamp on the original?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: This document reached us by packet radio communication. It was received in the communication centre, as can be seen from the incoming stamp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain why Mijo Bozic could not send this report by packet?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: The explanation is indicative of the situation we found ourselves in. When we had physically separated enclaves and the communications system was unsafe, passage was impossible, and for those reasons, they were not able to give us the document that we required by our order of 7 April, 1993. Because it is impossible to pass through physically, and if the communications do not guarantee the confidentiality of the document and the secrecy of the document, then the only correct way to act, for a military man, is to inform his superior that the assignment received cannot be carried out. This was a document drafted by Mijo Bozic, and it was normal for him to do so, because he was a professional soldier, and he knows how the structure of command and control functions and that the superior has to be informed about what is happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. Next document, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D255, D255A for the French version, D255B for the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: It must be 254.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You may continue, Mr. Nobilo. I'm sorry, Mr. Registrar, for interrupting.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: For the record, this is D254, D254A for the French version, D254B for the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can we have it on the ELMO? The document is very brief, and I'm going to read it, but I consider it to be extremely important.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Croatian Defence Council Headquarters, in addition to the number, we have the date, "Mostar, 24 August, 1993, military secret, strictly confidential, urgently sent to Kiseljak and Vitez." The heading is "Preparing of Actions." It is addressed to Tiho and Rajic, and the text reads: "Act urgently on the coordination regarding the group actions in the direction Kiseljak-Busovaca. Execute mutual connections and consultations," signed, "Croatian Defence Council Headquarters, General Major Milivoj Petkovic." We have the seal, indicating that it was received by packet. For the needs of the Court, could you tell us who Milivoj Petkovic is, where is the main headquarters, and where it is based?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: General Milivoj Petkovic, at the time, was Chief of Staff of the Main Headquarters of the HVO based in Posulsa.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is he the number one military man in the HVO?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes. This is the highest level of command, the main headquarters of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then it is addressed to Tiho and Rajic. Who is "Tiho" and who is "Rajic"?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: "Tiho" is General Blaskic, and "Rajic" is Ivica Rajic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was Ivica Rajic at the time?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: At the time, he was Commander of Operative Group 2 based in Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain, how is it possible that the main commander should simultaneously send an order to the commander of the Operative Zone and his subordinate? Isn't that quite contrary to what you said? Doesn't that undermine the chain of command as regulated in the army?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes, it does, but our physical separation and inability of the commander of the Operative Zone to extend any kind of assistance, to have any insight regarding the situation at the battlefront in Kiseljak, prompted the chief of staff of the main headquarters to issue such an order. Therefore, this order is the product of the situation in place at the time. By this order, the commander is placing, on the same level, the commander of the Operative Zone and the commander of the Operative Group, because the situation in the theatre was such that the commander of Operative Group 2 in Kiseljak had to assume responsibility for all defence operations and responsibility for the overall situation in that enclave, that is, in Operative Group 2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, are you familiar with the contents of this document when you received it in the Operative Zone, and do you recognise the incoming seal of the Operative Zone?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: I recognise the seal but not the contents, but parts of it I'm familiar with because, at the morning briefing, General Tihomir Blaskic informed us of this, and I even have a note in my diary about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In military terms, is it acceptable for a commander to say, "Act urgently on the coordination," or "Carry out mutual consultations"? Is that the wording used between superiors and subordinates or between two equals?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: This is not a relationship between superiors and subordinates, but between equal levels of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: New document, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D255, D255A for the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, by way of introduction, this document has been obtained by the Defence. It is a daily newspaper, Slobodna Dalmacija, the issue dated Thursday, the 7th of December, 1995, when an exclusive interview was published with Ivica Rajic. I should like to draw your attention to only a part of that text. I will read it, because it's not lengthy, and we would like to inform the Brigadier of this and hear his opinion. It is on page 3 of the translation under the sub-heading "The Clash with Blaskic." With your permission, I will read it: "The officials of The Hague Tribunal have stated on several occasions that Kresimir Zubak, when visiting the Tribunal, promised them your extradition. What do you know about this?" That is the journalist's question. "Answer: As far as I'm aware, Zubak promised cooperation with The Hague Tribunal, but whether there was a specific conversation about me, that I do not know. Question: There have occasionally been public suggestions, and even during the main hearing, that your clash with General Tihomir Blaskic, which dates back to as early as 1992, lay behind your arrest and the arrest of Dominik Iljasevic and Vlatko Trogrlic." Ivica Rajic answers: "The course of events in Kiseljak separated the two of us. We had our duels, both verbal and professional, as well as disagreements about our work. Blaskic had a totally different approach. I am a person who wants to be close to the people, close to the soldiers, fighters, and, unlike him, I am not interested in a career. The difference between him and me is that I'm ready to sacrifice my career for the people, whereas Blaskic is always ready to sacrifice the people for his career." The most important part of this, the point of my reading this interview: "In the beginning, Blaskic was my superior, but later, he was transferred to Vitez, while I remained in Kiseljak. Although Blaskic was formally my superior even then, the conditions on the ground imposed a situation where he and I were equally responsible to the main staff of the HVO, he for his sector, and I for mine. Blaskic wanted to cover up all the weaknesses that he carries inside himself, and which I warned the authorities about and tried to make those of us in Kiseljak out to be what the trial claimed we were." By way of an explanation, you will see that Rajic and his comrades were tried, and he gave this interview after this trial. "But he did not succeed in this. On several occasions, I attempted to clear up these relations with him and, in the end, I tried to make sure that our paths no longer crossed, in the interests of the Croatian people and in the interests of Kiseljak, which is where both of us come from. I did my utmost to avoid any kind of confrontation. All of those attempts came from my side, but Blaskic did not respond to them. He did not think it through maturely and, in the end, he did not draw the proper conclusions." In the next passage, which is entitled, "Cooked up in the Same Kitchen." The answer given by Rajic to the question; "You have been accused of being a trustworthy KOS man, counterintelligence service of the JNA." His answer is: "This was cooked up -- or sorry, all of this was directed against the legendary Maturica and Apostola units and only later against their commanders."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, do you know that there was a trial of Ivica Rajic in Mostar, he was acquitted and after that he granted this interview? Have you read this interview?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes, I know him because we met in 1992 when the front-line was being established after the fall of Jajce in the area of Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very briefly, the text will be read by the Judges, so we will not continue reading it, but just tell us what I have read just now about the responsibility, the fact of responsibility about both Blaskic and Rajic, each one for his own sector, was it really as Rajic stated here?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes, it was really so, when it came to the functioning of the command and control system.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could we have the next document, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 256, 256A for the English translation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We are not going to go into the essence of this document, I am just going to point out certain of its features and after that I will ask you for an opinion. From Fojnica, which originally belonged to Zubiniski, and Busovaca is sending to the defence department, medical sector, Colonel Rajic a report on the medical situation in his battalion, on the health situation. What does this tell you about the direct links between the Kiseljak enclave and Mostar?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: This speaks about a very difficult situation in which we were. Those kinds of situations would always require the need for some reports and information to be sent directly to Mostar because it was practically useless to send it to Vitez as we were not able to help them with those matters. Something even more important, that does not only mean that through direct chain of command a communication was established between the main headquarters and the command of the operative group, but we can also see from here that in other domains, like the medical domain, for example, direct communication had been established with those people that covered that particular matter, or particular portfolio in the ministry, that is the government.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could I ask for some help with the next document now.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is marked 257, 257A for the English translation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We are not going to read the whole document now, Brigadier, but just its title. The medical service of Ban Josip Jelacic Brigade is sending to the Mostar medical sector a report on the situation. We don't have the end of that report, but could you comment on whether this document is indicative of what you were telling us, that is the direct link with the services of the main command?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes, this is practically the confirmation of this type of communicating and cooperating with the main headquarters, the one that we've seen in the previous document. But also, this report shows how difficult the situation was. That there were wounded, that urgent help was needed. Obviously that was directly sent to the sector for health which was directly in charge of the wounded of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. We should now distribute another document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document is marked D258, 258A for the French version and 258B for the English version.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, I am only -- we are not going to read this document. Let me just briefly say that this document is the one that we believe was signed by Tihomir Blaskic and you're going to tell us that was dated the 11th of April, 1993 at 11.00 hours. From that, the British Battalion in Novi Bila, escort is asked from Kiseljak to Busovaca for a military delegation of ten members. Could you please tell the Court from when and until when you could in such a way, that is escorted by the British, that means the United Nation forces, travel between Busovaca and Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: This document was issued in the command of the Operative Zone and it was signed by Zoran Pilacic on behalf of the commander of the Operative Zone who had authorised him to do so. From January --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What year?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: 1993. After the area of Kacuni was cut off by the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the road to Kiseljak for the Croats and the HVO officers was not -- the Croats and the HVO officers could not go through the road. If you wanted to go to Kiseljak, you had to contact UNPROFOR so that they would be responsible for your security and escort you to Kiseljak. That situation happened in January, 1993, and such a situation continued up until the Washington Agreement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, during war operation, was the passage through this road possible at all, for example, during the war in April?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: It was not possible to go through it at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please tell the Court, did the British accept to escort HVO officers when they were performing combat duties or only for escorting them when they were going to meetings or negotiations?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: We never contacted the British for carrying out any military or combat missions. We asked for their help when we were going to various meetings, but more often than not organised by the UNPROFOR itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you go in your own vehicles, or did you have to go with UNPROFOR vehicles?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes, we had to go into armoured vehicles, I did it personally myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We have finished now discussing about this particular issue, although we're going to talk about it with another witness later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think that we have finished our working week now. I hope that you will have a good rest during the weekend and we will resume on Monday at 2.00 p.m. Please, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, just respectfully, if the first two charts that the Brigadier was talking about, 1 and 1A, if we could have some hard copies of those, I think it would be helpful. The two slides that the Brigadier was talking about, if we could get copies of those, please, I would appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have already asked that these maps be printed out and I hope that the Prosecution will soon have the copies of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's fine, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: When do you think you'll have these copies?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The slide earlier, we have to rely on the technical staff to make the first copy, which they have to print out from the computer material and then we can photocopy in colour, additional copies. As soon as I get the first copy, within a few hours, we can make additional copies to distribute. We're happy to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Have you heard the answer, Mr. Kehoe? So we'll see you on Monday at 2.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: 1.30 p.m., to be reconvened on Monday, the 28th day of September, 1998, at 2.00 p.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
